title: November 2026 Construction Material Prices: Are Your Estimates Still Accurate?
summary: See what November 2026 construction material prices mean for your next bid. Recheck supplier quotes, update allowances, and protect your remodeling margin.
body_markdown:
November 2026 Construction Material Prices: Are Your Estimates Still Accurate?


You’re ready to send a remodeling proposal, but the countertop quote expired last Friday, and the homeowner is still choosing appliances. The estimate looks finished, even though those costs could still change.


A call to the fabricator and a closer look at the appliance allowance can show whether your price still holds. In the example below, those checks uncover another $1,650 in project costs.


What are construction material prices doing in November 2026?


The National Association of Home Builders tracks what it costs to build new homes. Its October 15 report showed that the cost of goods and services rose 2% in September 2026. That was 10.3% higher than a year before. The cost of goods alone rose 1.8% in September.


## Handoff's November 2026 Retail Materials Snapshot


Through November 3, Handoff’s tracked retail materials index stood at 101.18 against a July 2026 baseline of 100. That puts the tracked basket 1.18% above the baseline. Check which materials affect your project before changing the estimate total.


## What do those price changes mean for your estimate?


A national or retail material price index doesn't tell you what your local fabricator will charge for a quartz countertop installation.


It also doesn't account for selected products, purchasing relationships, delivery charges, local inventory, or subcontractor labor. But it can tell you when it's worth revisiting an assumption.


Consider two remodeling projects. One contractor finalized pricing with suppliers yesterday and has written confirmation that the quotes will remain valid for another 30 days. Another contractor is using prices collected six weeks ago, with several homeowner selections still open.


Both may be looking at the same national trends, but their actual exposure is very different. The supplier quote, not the price index, should determine what changes in a specific estimate.


## Seven material categories to recheck before bidding


**1. Countertops**


Ask the shop to price the counters from the latest kitchen plans. Confirm whether the quote includes templating, fabrication, delivery, and installation, and how long it holds.


**2. Appliances**


A built-in fridge may need a different cabinet. A new cooktop may need new wiring. Send the model numbers to the people doing the work so they can check their prices. If the homeowner is still choosing, base the appliance allowance on the models they’re considering and confirm whether those selections change the cabinet or electrical scope.


**3. Wood and framing**


Check the latest plans before you order wood. A new wall or a larger opening may call for more lumber, a bigger beam, or different connectors or structural hardware.


**4. Electrical work**


Send your electrician the latest plans for lights and appliances. Ask if the price covers any new wires, circuits, or work at the breaker panel.


**5. Plumbing**


Give your plumber the model numbers for tubs, faucets, and showers. Ask if the parts will arrive on time and if you need to change any pipes before you close up the walls.


**6. Floors and tile**


Price the floor the homeowner picked. Add enough for cuts and waste. Ask your installer what it costs to prep the floor and lay the new tile or wood. A new tile pattern can take longer to lay.


**7. Heating and cooling**


Ask the crew to check the size, price, and arrival date of the new equipment. Find out if their price covers changes to ducts or vents. Check the same details for a new water heater.


**What happens when the price goes up?**


Say the countertop shop gave you a price on October 9. It was good through October 30. When you call on November 5, the shop wants $13,450 for the same work. That’s $950 more than the old price. The appliances the homeowner is looking at would add another $700.


Now say you planned to charge $200,000 for the job. Your estimate said the work would cost you $160,000. That left $40,000 in gross profit, the money left after you pay for the job itself. You still have to pay your business bills out of that money.


If you keep the price at $200,000, you lose $1,650 of the profit you planned to make. Your gross margin drops from 20% to about 19.2%. Gross margin is the share of the sale price left after you pay for the work.


With those updated costs, a selling price of $202,062.50 would maintain the planned 20% gross margin. You get that number by dividing the new job cost, $161,650, by 0.80. If the homeowner has already signed, check the agreement before you bring up a new price.

When to check your prices again


Save each supplier quote with the estimate line it supports. Record:


- The supplier’s name and contact
- The quote date and expiration
- What’s included and excluded
- The estimate line using that price


Check whether the quote will still hold when you expect to order. If the homeowner takes longer to decide or changes a selection, reconfirm the affected costs before committing to the price.


Before ordering, confirm availability and delivery timing too. A price you can still buy at won’t help the schedule if the material arrives late.

How to update material costs in a Handoff estimate


Once the fabricator confirms the new countertop price, open the project estimate and find the package you originally carried. Check that the revised quote covers the same scope before replacing the cost.


The steps below follow that update through to the proposal.


**1. Check the store price**


Handoff can use prices from supported Home Depot and Lowe’s catalogs when those catalogs are turned on. If you have a written price for your job, use it and check what it covers.


[How Handoff prices an estimate](https://help.handoff.ai/en/articles/9564039-how-handoff-prices-an-estimate)


**2. Call the supplier**


Ask when the price expires and what comes with it. If the homeowner is still picking appliances, check the models they’re looking at and see if any other crew needs to change its price.


**3. Enter the new cost**


Change the number yourself or ask Handy to do it. Here’s what you could type.


“Update the countertop package from $12,500 to $13,450. The new quote includes fabrication and installation. Flag any separate installation charge so I can check for double-counting, then show the revised total.”


[How to edit a line in Handoff](https://help.handoff.ai/en/articles/9778413-how-to-edit-items-on-an-estimate)


**4. Check what you’ll make**


Open the cost and profit summary. See what’s left after you pay for the work. Check whether the revised selling price still supports your target gross margin.


5. Read the proposal


Look at the copy the homeowner will see. Check the total, what the allowance covers, and how long the price is good for.


[How to make a proposal in Handoff](https://help.handoff.ai/en/articles/9504355-how-to-create-a-proposal)


## How to explain material price changes to homeowners


Explain the specific change while the homeowner can still choose what to do. For the countertop example, that might sound like:


“The quote for your counters expired while we were putting the proposal together. The updated price is $950 higher for the same quartz and installation. We can keep your selection or look at another option closer to the original budget.”


Keep the refreshed quote handy so you can show where the difference came from. If they bring up a cheaper proposal, compare what each includes before discussing a discount.


Read more about[explaining material price changes](https://www.handoff.ai/blog/how-to-talk-about-material-price-changes-before-your-client-asks) and[walking homeowners through a higher bid](https://www.handoff.ai/blog/how-to-justify-a-higher-bid-when-the-homeowner-has-three-others) .


## Frequently Asked Questions About Handoff and Material Prices


Are all material prices going up?


Prices can change by item and by store. Handoff’s tracked retail materials basket was 1.18% above its July baseline on November 3. Call your supplier for the price on the items you need.


How long is a quote good for?


Look for a date on the written quote. If you don’t see one, ask the supplier how long they’ll hold the price.


What if the homeowner hasn’t picked a product?


Use an allowance based on the products they’re considering. State whether it includes delivery and installation, and explain how a different selection could affect the price.


Can Handoff update my estimate?


Yes. Enter the new cost yourself or ask Handy to change it. Check the new total and margin before you send the proposal.


What’s the difference between markup and margin?


Say a part costs you $100 and you sell it for $125. The extra $25 is 25% of your cost. That’s your markup. The same $25 is 20% of the sale price. That’s your gross margin.


## Check your next bid in Handoff


Open the estimate that’s been waiting longest for a homeowner decision. Check the supplier quotes behind its highest costs and update anything that no longer holds.


In Handoff, you can revise those lines with your AI assistant and review the margin before sending the proposal. Keep the confirmed quotes with the project so you have the numbers behind the price.
